Here is a small problem that every office has. After a meeting, somebody asks you what was said, and you have to pass it on. In English, you do this with two verbs, say and tell. They mean almost the same thing, but they work differently. You say something, but you tell somebody something. So you can say, Paul said that the report was ready, or Paul told me that the report was ready. You cannot say Paul said me. The second thing to notice is the tense. When you report, the verb usually moves back in time. Paul says, I am busy, and you report, Paul said that he was busy. Paul says, I will call you, and you report, he said that he would call. Do not worry about getting it perfect. Your colleagues will understand you. But if you get say and tell right, you will sound much more natural in every meeting.

Hi Janderson, it is Tom Becker from the Miami office. I am sorry I missed you this morning. I am calling about your client, Mr. Alves. I spoke to him yesterday afternoon, and he told me three things. First, he said that he was happy with the fund, but he wanted a lower fee next year. Second, he said that his daughter was moving to Boston in the summer, and that she would need an account there. And third, he told me that he could not come to the meeting on Friday, because he was traveling. I promised him that you would call him back this week. Could you send me a short update after you speak to him? Thanks a lot. Talk soon.
